content.p: On 21 September 2026 two students at the University of Mississippi, known as Ole Miss, were found dead in Oxford within about an hour of each other. Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old freshman from Englewood, Colorado, was found on campus. Robert Strang, a 20-year-old junior from Atlanta, was found at a house near campus. Police were called to each by a separate report of someone unresponsive and possibly overdosing. In both rooms investigators found opened packets of the same product: tablets sold as "Smax Pseudo-DHM", a synthetic relative of the herbal drug kratom, whose label listed an ingredient that the federal government had banned less than a month before.

Investigators traced Hamilton's purchases to a vape shop in Oxford. On 2 October 2026 federal prosecutors charged the shop's manager and his 18-year-old son with possessing a controlled substance with intent to distribute it. Neither man is accused of causing either death, and as of early October investigators had not said what killed the two students. Federal prosecutors said both deaths appeared consistent with overdoses.

According to a sworn statement filed by local narcotics investigators, police received two separate calls on 21 September. The first led them to Hamilton on campus; Fox News reported that he is believed to have died in Stewart Hall, a dormitory. An official noted that he "could have died due to a Pulmonary Edema", a buildup of fluid in the lungs that is consistent with an overdose. About an hour later officers were sent to a house near campus, where Strang was found "cold to the touch".

Near Hamilton investigators found packages of suspected kratom derivatives, some with tablets missing. On Strang's nightstand was a packet of the same Smax tablets. According to court documents described by Fox News, it sat beside 20 to 30 small nitrous oxide canisters, which his roommates said he used daily. They also told officers he had taken a Xanax bar the day before he was found.

The university named the two students on 24 September. "Aidan was a bright, wonderful young man who was taken too soon," his family said. Strang's family thanked friends for an outpouring of love and support and asked for privacy. A university vice chancellor urged students not to speculate. Oxford police said they had no confirmed information that kratom or any other substance had contributed to either death, but told people to avoid it "out of an abundance of caution", and noted that Narcan, which can reverse an overdose, was available on campus.

Kratom comes from a tree native to Southeast Asia. In small amounts it acts as a stimulant and in larger ones as a sedative. Plain kratom leaf is legal under federal law, and its supporters say it helps people with pain, anxiety and opioid withdrawal. The concern, even among its advocates, is with concentrated and synthetic derivatives. Eleven states have banned kratom outright. Mississippi regulates it, chiefly by requiring buyers to be at least 21. Oxford has banned its sale, possession and use since 2019, and Lafayette County, which includes Oxford, since 2021.

The packets found in Oxford were labelled Smax Pseudo-DHM, carried the brand name Modus, and listed pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15 (DHM) among their ingredients. On 26 August 2026 the Drug Enforcement Administration had temporarily placed mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in Schedule I, which bars its sale. A Mississippi investigator said in court papers that he believed the "pseudoindoxyl" on the label referred to that compound, and laboratory tests of the tablets were pending. The investigators described the product as a kratom-like substance sold in petrol stations and tobacco shops, which people buy for its "narcotic like effect".

A senior fellow of the American Kratom Association, Mac Haddow, said these tablets were not natural kratom leaf and that students should have been warned specifically about them. Fox News reported that the Smax Pseudo tablets were not listed on the Modus website and that the company had not answered its calls and emails.

Hamilton's bank records showed that during September he had bought from Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford more than once, most recently the day before he died. On 24 September the Lafayette County Metro Narcotics unit sent a confidential informant, carrying hidden recording equipment, into the shop to ask whether it sold 7-OH kratom pills.

According to the affidavit of Michael Dassance, a special agent of the DEA, the clerk, Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, said yes and took a packet from a drawer under the register. When other customers came in he told the informant to be quiet and pushed the pills out of sight, and when they left he finished the sale. He warned the informant to "be careful taking the pills because people were dying from them," the affidavit said.

Officers searched the shop the same day. They seized more than 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products, valued in the affidavit at $1,799, along with THC cartridges, gummies and other cannabis products. Among them, WMC reported, was the same Smax Mango Breeze product found near Hamilton, in identical packaging, with the same ingredients and the same $39.99 price sticker, smudged on the 9. Mosleh, 51, the shop's manager, and his son, Islam Yahya Mosleh, 18, who had been serving customers, were arrested and charged under state law with possessing Schedule I drugs with intent to distribute. Each was held on $100,000 bond. At that stage officials said they had not established any connection with the deaths.

Investigators also went through Strang's financial records. They showed purchases at Express Mart #7, a petrol station convenience store in Yalobusha County, on 9 and 11 September. Reports placed it about 20 miles, or about 30 minutes' drive, from Oxford. Officers bought similar pills there and sent them to a laboratory. Its owner told Fox News Digital that the packet found by Strang's bed did not come from his store, because he does not put price stickers on his stock and that packet had one. He did not dispute that his store had sold Smax tablets, and said federal agents had seized all his kratom products. As of 29 September no one at that business had been arrested or charged.

On 2 October US Attorney Scott F. Leary of the Northern District of Mississippi announced a criminal complaint against the father and son, connecting the case to Hamilton's death. The Justice Department said investigators had found a "suspected link" between the packets in the students' rooms and the shop. At a hearing on 1 October a magistrate judge found there was enough evidence for the charges. Their lawyers, Scott Davis for the father and A.E. Harlow Jr. for the son, declined to comment.

In a motion asking that both men be kept in custody, prosecutors described them as a danger to the community. The filing said toxicology tests on both students had found mitragynine, MGM-15 and MGPI, the same substances found in the Smax Mango Breeze pills, and alleged that Puffs had sold Hamilton the pills twice in the days before his death. It also said a school resource officer at Oxford High School, where the younger Mosleh is a student, had previously suspected him of selling THC vapes to other students, and that similar vapes were found in his pockets and backpack.

A former federal prosecutor, Neama Rahmani, told Fox News that anyone who sells a Schedule I drug breaks the law, but that a prosecution must prove intent, and that a manufacturer could also face civil and criminal liability if its product contained a banned substance.

Mississippi's governor, Tate Reeves, said the state Department of Public Safety and Bureau of Narcotics were helping local police and working to speed up the toxicology reports. "Please talk to your children about this situation and the dangers associated with taking illegal drugs," he wrote. A state spokesman said the reports would be finished "in due course" and that the families would hear the results first. Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said the investigation remained active and that more charges were possible, and Oxford police warned sellers to expect a visit. "We will investigate. We will obtain warrants. We will seize illegal products, and we will hold those responsible accountable," they said.

Authorities have said they have no evidence that the two deaths were connected to each other. Whether the tablets caused either death, and who made them, had not been established by early October 2026.
